title: WireCraft
subtitle: A Simulation Benchmark for Industrial DLO Manipulation
secondaryVenue: Also presented as an oral at the IROS 2026 DOM-R3 Workshop
affiliations: Department of Mechanical and Industrial Engineering, University of Toronto, Canada
CREFLE Inc., Seongnam, Republic of Korea
intro: A wire bends, drags, and catches on the fixtures around it. WireCraft studies how robots handle these interactions through connector insertion, clip routing, and channel seating. The benchmark combines configurable simulation tasks with demonstrations and evaluation on a physical UR5.
abstract: Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs), such as wires and cables, are central to industrial assembly. Unlike rigid objects, whose state is captured by a 6-DoF pose, DLOs have an infinite-dimensional configuration space and deform continuously under contact with grippers, fixtures, and the workspace, making them a demanding benchmark for general dexterous manipulation. Despite their importance, policy development and comparison remain difficult: existing benchmarks are often tied to specific hardware setups, lack modular and customizable task assets, or study generic deformable-object tasks without the fixtures relevant to real-world industrial wire manipulation. Few benchmarks align simulation, real-world data, and shared evaluation protocols. To bridge this gap, we introduce WireCraft, a simulation benchmark for industrial DLO manipulation with configurable difficulty and assets, spanning three task families: connector insertion, clip routing, and channel seating. It supports two complementary DLO physics models, articulated and deformable, and the released trajectories come from both simulation and a physical UR5. We benchmark reinforcement learning (RL), imitation learning (IL), and vision-language-action (VLA) policies under shared metrics. Privileged state-based RL solves a representative setting in each task family with over 82% success, confirming the tasks are well-posed. Image-based policies remain less successful across the evaluated tasks, with ACT and DiT VLA falling below privileged State PPO. On a physical UR5, supplementing real demonstrations with simulated data improves success by 15–65 percentage points in the best-performing mixture for each task. These results indicate that industrial DLO manipulation, though tractable under privileged state, remains an open challenge for current vision-based learning.

method.description: Built on Isaac Sim 4.5 and Isaac Lab 2.2.1, WireCraft combines industrial task fixtures with articulated rigid-body and finite-element deformable wire models. A shared dataset schema connects simulated and physical demonstrations to policy training.

media.alt: WireCraft architecture: simulation engine, industrial wire and fixture assets, task generation, demonstration sources, learning policies, and physical robot evaluation.
media.caption: The paper’s architecture diagram. Physical evaluation now covers all three task families, with results below.

points.title: Configurable physical tasks
points.description: Vary connector geometry and socket clearance, clip layout, or channel shape. The same task definitions are used to evaluate policy success.

points.title: Two wire representations
points.description: Articulated rigid-body chains support parallel data generation; finite-element deformable wires model local bending and contact deformation.

points.title: Shared learning interfaces
points.description: Reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and vision-language-action policies use task-specific observations. UR5 trajectories share a LeRobot v3.0 format.

results.realSummary: Adding simulated demonstrations improves observed task success on the physical UR5. The best mixture for each task increases success by 65 percentage points for insertion, 20 for routing, and 15 for seating, compared with real demonstrations alone.
results.realProtocol: Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) on a physical UR5 with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper. Each task and data mixture is evaluated over 20 trials. Checkpoints are selected by lowest action error on held-out real episodes. Every mixture includes real demonstrations.

insertionMedia.alt: Simulated Ethernet-style insertion: privileged State PPO and SACfD exceed 92% insertion success; all image-based policies have a gap between reaching the socket and completing insertion.
insertionMedia.caption: Simulation · Ethernet-style connector, deformable wire, 3 mm socket clearance. Reach and insert are separate success metrics; error bars show standard deviation.

results.scope: The hardware study uses a UR5 with one fixture configuration per task and narrower randomization than simulation. Training-set size changes with data mixture, so these results do not isolate source diversity from data volume. They do not measure zero-shot transfer.
